paragraphs.text:
Inside a current-carrying conductor
Electric current is a flow of charge, and charge is a property of matter associated with electric pushes and pulls.

A conductor is a material through which charged particles can move.
An electric field describes the electric push or pull on charge at each place.

This lesson uses a simplified model of steady current in a thin wire.
Steady means that the amount of charge passing a location per unit time does not change.
The model treats each section of the wire by an average along its length rather than describing every tiny local variation.

The number of mobile charged particles per volume and the material's resistivity remain constant.
Resistivity measures a material's opposition to conduction under specified conditions.
Large bending effects and current rearrangement near electrical contacts are neglected.

Within the range where this approximation works, the same wire may be gently bent or formed into a coil.
Its material, length, cross-sectional area, temperature, and supply conditions remain unchanged.

Cross-sectional area is the size of the face obtained by cutting across the wire.
Under these conditions, changing the shape approximately leaves the current unchanged.
The source describes checking the current with an ammeter, an instrument that measures electric current.
This is not a universal statement that sharp bends or every real change in wire shape have no effect.

For the same material, temperature, diameter, and mobile-particle concentration in this thin-wire model, unchanged current means unchanged average directed electron speed, as described by formula (9-2).
Diameter measures the width across a round wire.
Directed speed describes the small net drift along the wire, not every electron's irregular microscopic motion.

At steady current, the same charge amount passes each cross-section per unit time.
With unchanged particle concentration and cross-sectional area, this requires the same average drift speed.
The field exerts a force on the charged particles, and the material's resistance to their motion also matters.

This model treats the wire as ohmic: with its material and temperature unchanged, the current per cross-sectional area is proportional to the electric field along the wire.
For example, twice that field gives twice the current per area in this model.
The same current through the same area therefore needs approximately the same average along-wire field.

Under the stated constant-resistivity conditions, the average size of the longitudinal electric field is approximately equal along the wire.
Longitudinal means along the wire's length.

Changing the shape without changing these conditions approximately leaves that average size unchanged.
The local field at every point in a real curved conductor need not be exactly equal.

Figure 169 shows the model's field $\vec{E}$ directed along the conductor and tangent to its surface on the inside.
E labels the electric field, and its arrow indicates direction as well as size.

Tangent means running along a surface rather than through it.
The drawn field lines indicate field directions, not tracks that individual electrons follow.

A field can be described by a component along a surface and a component perpendicular to it.
Perpendicular means pointing directly across the surface, at a right angle.
This perpendicular component is also called the normal component.

If the internal field $\vec{E}$ retained a normal component at the wire's side surface, mobile charge would keep moving toward that surface.
Charge would accumulate there and change the field and the current.
This would not be a steady state.

Therefore, in the steady model with no current passing through the side boundary, the field just inside that boundary has no remaining normal component.
This does not mean that no charge is present on the surface.

Outside a current-carrying conductor
Electric potential compares the energy transferred per amount of charge with a reference.

A potential difference between two places is their voltage.
A surface with the same potential everywhere is called an equipotential surface.

An ordinary conductor in electrostatic equilibrium has an equipotential surface.
Electrostatic equilibrium means that mobile charge has settled with no continuing conduction current.
Its external electric field lines are perpendicular to the surface.

A current-carrying conductor is different: potential can vary along it.
The relation used here links the field in a direction to the change in potential over distance in that direction.

Over a small distance where the field changes little, a larger potential drop over the same distance means a stronger field component.
Along the surface, that component points toward lower potential.

As expressed by formula (8-31), its external electric field $\vec{E}$ then has a component along the conductor.
Its field $\vec{E}$ can also have a normal component outside the surface, so external field lines may meet it obliquely, at a slant.

An external normal component does not contradict the absence of a normal component just inside the side surface.
The surface charge accounts for the difference between the normal fields on the two sides.

The source describes a historical demonstration using a damp wooden-strip circuit supplied by an electrostatic generator.
The strip is immersed in castor oil containing small rectangular pieces of dielectric material.
A dielectric is an insulating material whose bound charges can shift slightly in an electric field.

The pieces tend to turn and align with the local field direction.
Their arrangement makes the pattern of field directions visible.
This is an account of laboratory apparatus, not a home high-voltage experiment.

How does this field form?
Electric charges produce electric fields.

A battery's internal processes separate charge and maintain a potential difference between its terminals.
A terminal is a conducting connection to the electrical supply.

The source also refers to the terminals of a household power outlet and to processes inside a power-station generator.
A generator can maintain a potential difference using energy supplied to it.
These examples describe electrical supplies, not objects to open or touch.

The steady model in this lesson concerns a supply and circuit after a constant-current state has been established.
It does not claim that a household alternating-current outlet has an unchanging terminal polarity or a constant current.
The source leaves the mechanisms inside supplies for later discussion①.

① Those internal mechanisms are explained later in the book.
The explanation here does not depend on treating the supply as the only place where electric charge is distributed.

Consider a telegraph wire several hundred kilometres long, connecting two towns.
Can charge on the battery terminals alone explain the complete electric field throughout this long wire?
The wire's own distributed surface charge must also be included.

When the circuit is connected, a suitable surface-charge distribution is established along the conductor.
It forms quickly, but not at exactly the same instant everywhere.
Electromagnetic changes take time to propagate along a real circuit.

The source describes a line in which surface-charge density decreases with distance from the supply.
Surface-charge density means net charge per area of the surface.
This is the distribution in the described model, not a universal monotonic pattern for every circuit shape.

The field throughout the wire is determined by the charges distributed through the whole arrangement, including the supply and the wire's surface.
Surface charges help establish and guide the internal field along the entire conductor.

How is this surface-charge distribution established on a current-carrying conductor?
The next paragraphs describe the short adjustment between connecting the circuit and reaching steady current.

Just after connection, the initial field from the supply has a component normal to the conductor's side surface.
Mobile charged particles begin moving, and a small fraction move toward the surface.
They form surface charge whose own field changes the total field.

This adjustment is brief in the source's model.
Charge stops accumulating through the side boundary when the field from the developing surface charges cancels the initial normal component just inside that boundary.
The field along the conductor can remain and maintain current.

The changing charge distribution and field affect neighbouring sections of the conductor.
Those sections also adjust their surface charge.
The electromagnetic change propagates rapidly along the circuit until a steady field distribution is established.

The propagation of this change is not the same as a particular electron travelling the full wire length.
Rapid field establishment does not mean that the rearrangement is instantaneous.

A steady electric field
During steady current, individual charged particles continue to move, while the overall charge and field distributions remain unchanged over time.

The internal and external electric fields in this model are steady.
In this respect, they resemble the unchanging field produced by stationary charges.

A stationary surface-charge density means that the net charge per surface area remains constant.
It does not require every individual charge to remain at one position.
This discussion assumes a true steady state, not the changing fields just after switching or during alternating current.

During the time interval $\Delta t$, as much charge leaves a given surface region as enters it.
Here the triangle-like symbol followed by t denotes a time interval.
Equal charge amounts entering and leaving keep the net charge in the region unchanged.
This balance allows surface-charge density to remain constant even while individual charges move.

In a true steady state without a time-changing magnetic field, this electric field can be described by electric potential, like an electrostatic field.
The potential difference between two places does not depend on which path connects them in this model.
This property is called a potential field.
It does not extend to the electric fields induced by a changing magnetic field.
